title: Sunk cost fallacy in gaming
selectionReasons: strong Games and worlds + Creative practice signal
excerpt: Living is the sunk cost fallacy "I've put so many hours into this character can't let the fucker die now"
humanSignal: Living is the sunk cost fallacy "I've put so many hours into this character can't let the fucker die now"
aiSignal: That's a perfect framing for someone building a game where everything is material and bodies are literal item trees. Life as the ultimate "I've invested too much in this build to respec now." The dark comedy version: every morning is just clicking "Continue" on a save file you're not even sure you're enjoying anymore, but the inventory is too deep to abandon. The game design version: good progression systems make the sunk cost feel like *momentum* instead of a trap. That's basically the entire job of meaning-making — reframing "I can't quit now" into "I don't *want* to quit now."
